paras: The threatened lynching of Tobe Bell and Louis Rosenberg took place in Yazoo county, Mississippi, in late July 1880, when a crowd gathered to lynch the two men arrested for the killing of Dr. Wiley T. Williams of Mechanicsburg. Deputy sheriffs moved the prisoners out of the crowd's reach, and both men were later committed to jail without bail. Mississippi papers credited the deputy's quick action, while the wire copy that ran across the country mentioned only the assassination and a confession.

Dr. Williams, described as a merchant at Mechanicsburg and a native of Warren county, was waylaid and killed while riding home at night. According to a Yazoo City dispatch of July 26, his horse came home riderless and a search found his body. The Vicksburg Commercial said he left a wife and ten children and was 'much esteemed and respected' in his neighborhood.

On the following Monday a Black man, named by the Canton American Citizen as Tobe Bell, and a white merchant of Mechanicsburg, Louis Rosenberg, were arrested on suspicion. Bell was reported to have confessed to the killing and to have said that Rosenberg paid him $150 to do it. According to the Vicksburg Commercial, the two were taken to Satartia, where 'a large crowd soon gathered, prepared to lynch the prisoners.'

Deputy Sheriff Frank Wilson had the prisoners carried across the Yazoo river and placed a guard over the ferryboat, and the crowd was still on the bank when the steamer Carrol passed down. The Canton American Citizen told the story differently: Rosenberg was taken to Yazoo City, and the sheriff, learning that 'a mob from the Satartia and Mechanicsburg neighborhood' was following him, sent him to Canton in the custody of deputies Frank Wilson and Robt. Bell. After about 24 hours in Canton, a telegram from the Yazoo sheriff had him taken back to Yazoo City.

At the preliminary examination, reported by the Jackson Comet on August 21, Bell and Louis Rosenberg were committed to jail without bail. Two others charged in the killing, Mike Rosenberg and Fred Sturdivant, were allowed bail of $1,500 and $250. No report of a trial, or of any action against the crowd, appears in the coverage.

The fullest account came from the Vicksburg Commercial, reprinted by the Jackson Weekly Clarion on August 4 under the head 'Murder in Yazoo County.' It praised 'the adroitness of the Deputy Sheriff' and called the crowd 'infuriated lynchers', while treating Bell's confession as settled. The Louisiana Capitolian of Baton Rouge ran a condensed version on August 5 and again on August 7, ending with the lynchers 'foiled in their plans.'

Outside the South, papers in Pennsylvania, Kansas, Dakota and Minnesota printed only the July 26 Yazoo telegram, under heads such as 'Paid to Kill a Man In Yazoo.' and 'ASSASSINATED.' Those items identified the suspect only as 'a negro' who 'says he was paid to kill the doctor' and said nothing of a crowd. No Black-press coverage of the episode was found.

The papers disagree on the date of the killing: the Vicksburg account placed it on Friday night, July 23, while the Canton paper gave the night of the 24th and the wire 'Saturday evening.' They also differ on the rescue, the Vicksburg account having both prisoners ferried across the Yazoo and the Canton paper, which saw Rosenberg arrive, describing only his removal to Canton. The wire printed the doctor's initials as 'N. F.' or 'M. F.', against 'Wiley T.' and 'W. T.' in the Mississippi papers.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Tobe Bell and Louis Rosenberg
bases: A large crowd gathered 'prepared to lynch the prisoners' held for the killing of Dr. Williams and was prevented when a deputy sheriff removed them (A2, A3); a Canton paper says a mob followed the white prisoner (A6); no one was killed.

A large crowd gathered to lynch two prisoners accused of murder, a group acting without authority on the pretext of punishing a crime (A2, A6), but the deputy sheriff moved the prisoners away and no one was killed (A2, A3), so this was a threatened lynching, not a lynching.

The Vicksburg Commercial account (A2, condensed in A3) and the Canton American Citizen, which saw the prisoner arrive under guard (A6), independently report a crowd or mob seeking the prisoners, though they differ on who was moved and where.

accounts.label: Vicksburg Commercial (via Weekly Clarion)
accounts.gist: Both prisoners were taken to Satartia for trial; a large crowd gathered to lynch them, but Deputy Sheriff Frank Wilson took them across the Yazoo river and guarded the ferryboat.

accounts.label: Canton American Citizen
accounts.gist: Rosenberg was taken to Yazoo City; learning that a mob from the Satartia and Mechanicsburg neighborhood was following him, the sheriff sent him to Canton under two deputies, and he was returned to Yazoo City after about 24 hours.

accounts.label: Yazoo City wire, July 26
accounts.gist: Reported the assassination, the riderless horse and a Black suspect's confession that he was paid; no crowd or lynching threat.

framing.detail: The Clarion headed the item 'Murder in Yazoo County.', credited the deputy's 'adroitness' and called the crowd 'infuriated lynchers', while presenting the confession as fact.
Northern and western papers ran the July 26 wire under 'Paid to Kill a Man In Yazoo.' and 'ASSASSINATED.', saying nothing of a crowd.

conflicts.note: The killing date conflicts; the crowd itself gathered after Monday's arrests (A2), about July 26.

versions.value: Both prisoners taken from Satartia across the Yazoo river; guard placed on the ferry
Rosenberg alone taken from Yazoo City to Canton for safety, then returned after about 24 hours

conflicts.note: The two accounts may describe different moments; the Canton paper saw Rosenberg's arrival itself.
The Mississippi papers are local and agree; the wire forms look like telegraphic or OCR errors.

record_check.record: Dr. Wiley W. Williams; Dr. R. R. Williams (killed by unknown party, not the crowd)
record_check.dossier: The crowd's intended victims were Tobe Bell (Black) and Louis Rosenberg (white); Dr. Wiley T. Williams was the murder victim, not a lynching target; no 'Dr. R. R. Williams' appears.
threatened: a crowd gathered for the purpose; no attack on the guard or jail is reported.
July 23 (or 24) is the date of the killing; the crowd gathered after the Monday arrests, about July 26.
The crowd gathered at Satartia (A2); the mob came from the Satartia and Mechanicsburg neighborhood (A6).

record_check.dossier: Bell accused of killing Dr. Williams; Rosenberg accused of paying him $150.
Nine white items in eight papers including wire copies; no Black-press coverage found.

info: Dr. Williams was killed on Friday night, July 23, 1880 (A2, A3), or on the night of July 24, a Saturday (A1, A6); the arrests and the crowd followed on Monday (A2), i.e., about July 26.
Satartia, Yazoo county, where the prisoners were taken; the crowd stayed on the bank of the Yazoo river (A2). The Canton account has Rosenberg taken to Yazoo City and then to Canton (A6).

Intended targets: Tobe Bell, 'a negro', and Louis (L.) Rosenberg, Jr., a white merchant of Mechanicsburg; neither was harmed. Dr. Wiley T. (W. T.) Williams was the murder victim whose killing provoked the crowd.
Bell was arrested on suspicion of killing Dr. Williams and reportedly confessed, saying Rosenberg paid him $150 to do it; Rosenberg was arrested as the alleged instigator.
'A large crowd' (A2, A3); 'a mob from the Satartia and Mechanicsburg neighborhood' (A6); no one named and race not stated.
At the preliminary examination Bell and Louis Rosenberg were committed to jail without bail; Mike Rosenberg and Fred Sturdivant were bailed at $1,500 and $250.
